summaries.example: Imagine two tennis players. One has practiced serving, but she is far from a court and has no racket. She has a general ability to serve. The other is on a court with a racket and ball, ready to serve. She also has a specific ability to serve right now. This shows that ability can mean a lasting skill or an action that is possible in the present situation.
summaries.summary: An ability is a special kind of power: it belongs to an agent and is connected to an action. People have ordinary abilities, such as walking or writing, and unusual abilities, such as playing difficult music. The entry asks what makes ability claims true. It separates abilities from dispositions, affordances, and other powers. It also distinguishes general abilities from specific abilities. A person may know how to perform an action or have practiced it, yet lack the chance to do it at this moment. Philosophers offer several explanations. One says that an agent has an ability when the agent would succeed if they tried. Other views appeal to possible situations, options, potentialities, or powers that work in two directions: an agent can use them or not. The entry also explains why abilities matter for debates about free will, responsibility, and disability. No single account is presented as settled.
key_ideas: People often make true claims about what others can do, so philosophers try to explain what abilities are.
Abilities are powers of agents that relate to actions. They are different from powers of ordinary objects, such as a glass being easy to break.
Having an ability may depend on more than wanting to act. A person might have a physical or psychological obstacle.
Some philosophers connect ability with what would happen if a person tried. Others explain ability using possibility, options, or special kinds of power.
Ability is connected to know-how, skill, free will, and disability, but the connections are debated.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use words such as “can,” “cannot,” and “is able to” all the time. Understanding these words can help us think more carefully about learning, practice, obstacles, choice, responsibility, and disability. It also reminds us that a person may have an ability even when circumstances prevent them from using it.

important_terms.definition: A power that belongs to an agent and connects that agent with an action, such as speaking, running, or drawing.
A property that makes something likely to act or change in a certain way, even when it is not doing so now.
A power or possibility that belongs to a thing or an agent. Abilities are one kind of power.
Knowing the way to do something. Philosophers disagree about whether this is the same as having an ability.
An ability that a person has generally, even when the needed opportunity or equipment is missing.
An ability that a person can use in the current situation, with the needed conditions in place.

questions_to_think_about: Is someone able to do something if they know how but cannot do it right now?
Does practicing always turn an ability into a skill?
Should a lucky success count as showing an ability?
What is the difference between being able to do something generally and being able to do it today?

summaries.example: Consider a skilled tennis player who is standing at the service line with a racket and ball. She may have the specific ability to serve now. A similar player who is highly trained but is far from a court may have the general ability to serve without having the specific ability at that moment. The distinction matters because a theory that explains present opportunity may not yet explain enduring competence.
summaries.summary: The philosophical problem of ability begins with a familiar fact: claims about what agents can do are often true, so they require an account rather than simple dismissal. The entry classifies abilities as powers of agents directed toward actions. This classification distinguishes them from dispositions, affordances, and other powers, while also inheriting difficult questions about agency and action. It then examines the relation between ability, know-how, and skill. A Rylean approach treats knowing how as closely tied to ability, whereas intellectualist approaches analyze know-how through knowledge of propositions; skill may additionally involve practice or strategic control. Formal distinctions are central. General ability can persist without an immediate opportunity, while specific ability concerns an agent’s present options. Global/local, simple/intentional, and narrow/wide distinctions mark further differences in range, control, and dependence on circumstances. The main theories are hypothetical and non-hypothetical. The conditional analysis links ability to what an agent would do if they tried, but psychological obstacles and failed attempts create counterexamples. Dispositional, success-based, and more complex conditional views respond in different ways. Modal analyses treat ability as restricted possibility, though lucky success and disjunctive cases create logical problems. Other theories appeal to potentialities, two-way powers, options, or obstacles. These theories are applied to free will, moral responsibility, and competing naturalistic or evaluative accounts of disability. The entry presents an active research problem rather than a final definition.
key_ideas: The entry treats abilities as agentive powers: they belong to agents and concern actions. This separates them from dispositions of objects and from agentive powers that do not concern action.

The relation between ability, know-how, and skill is unsettled. One view identifies know-how with ability; intellectualist views connect know-how to propositional knowledge; other accounts add practice or flexible control to ability.

General and specific ability are distinct but related. General ability concerns competence across relevant circumstances, while specific ability concerns what the agent can do given the circumstances at hand.

The conditional analysis claims, roughly, that an agent can perform an action if the agent would perform it were they to try. Counterexamples involve psychological barriers, failed attempts by competent agents, and the difference between general and specific ability.

More sophisticated hypothetical accounts revise the relevant volition or the counterfactual structure. Dispositional accounts treat abilities as related to dispositions, but critics argue that this may omit control or what is genuinely up to the agent.

Non-hypothetical approaches include modal analyses, potentiality theories, two-way powers, and option-based accounts. Problems include lucky success, disjunctive abilities, and the danger of explaining ability with another unexplained modal notion.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ability claims appear in theories of action, knowledge, freedom, responsibility, and disability. Small differences in what “can” means—general versus specific, controlled versus lucky, internal versus situation-dependent—can change the conclusions of larger arguments. A careful theory must therefore explain both the truth of ordinary ability claims and their role in these broader debates.

important_terms.definition: A power of an agent that relates the agent to an action. This definition leaves open difficult questions about what counts as an agent and an action.
A property of an object or agent that disposes it to behave in a certain way under suitable conditions; dispositions are one kind of power.
The broad category of possibilities or capacities inherent in things and agents, including dispositions, affordances, and abilities.
The view that knowing how to perform an action is, at least in some cases, knowing a proposition about a way of performing it.
An ability possessed across circumstances, even when the agent lacks the immediate opportunity to exercise it.
An ability an agent has in the present circumstances because relevant conditions and opportunities are in place.
A theory that analyzes ability through a counterfactual dependence between an agent’s volition and the agent’s action.
A broad family of views that explains ability using possibility, often represented with possible worlds and restrictions on which worlds count as relevant.

questions_to_think_about: Does a person who succeeds only by luck thereby show an ability?
Can an account of specific ability explain general ability, or must the order be reversed?
Does knowing how to ski require the physical ability to ski at this moment?
Can a possible-worlds account capture control without building ability into its restrictions?
Should theories of disability focus on species-normal abilities, socially expected abilities, or abilities important for justice and well-being?

summaries.example: A student has trained for months to give a difficult presentation. On presentation day, the projector fails and the student cannot show the slides. It still seems right that the student has a general ability to give the presentation, even though the student may lack the specific ability to give it in exactly the planned way at that moment. If the student freezes because of a severe fear, that also raises a question: is wanting to try enough for ability, or must the person be psychologically ready as well?
summaries.summary: The entry investigates what it means to say that someone can perform an action. Abilities are treated as powers of agents, not simply as dispositions of objects. An ability relates an agent to an action, although the boundaries of agency and action can be unclear. The discussion also separates ability from know-how and skill. Some philosophers defend a Rylean connection between knowing how and being able, while intellectualists say know-how involves knowing a proposition about a way to act. Skill may require practice or a flexible ability to adjust one’s actions. A major distinction is between general and specific ability. A trained tennis player far from a court can have the general ability to serve, while a player equipped and positioned to serve has the specific ability. Further distinctions concern how widely an ability applies, how much control it involves, and whether it depends on the agent alone or on the environment. The best-known hypothetical account is the conditional analysis: an agent can perform an action if the agent would do it when trying. Examples involving psychological obstacles and unsuccessful attempts challenge both its sufficiency and its necessity. More elaborate conditional and dispositional accounts try to repair these problems. Modal accounts analyze ability as a restricted form of possibility, but lucky successes and cases involving a choice between alternatives create difficulties. Other views use potentiality, two-way powers, options, or obstacles. Finally, theories of ability are applied to free will, moral responsibility, and disability. The entry surveys these proposals without treating the debate as settled.
key_ideas: The entry asks for a general theory of ability, not just a list of particular talents. It begins from the idea that ordinary ability claims are often meaningful and true.

Abilities are a type of power belonging to agents and directed toward actions. This makes them different from an object’s disposition or from a power to understand something if understanding is not itself an action.

Know-how and skill may be connected to ability but are not obviously identical to it. Some philosophers treat know-how as propositional knowledge, while others emphasize successful action, practice, or flexible control.
General and specific abilities explain why a person can be trained to do something without being able to do it in the present setting. Philosophers debate which kind is more basic.

Conditional theories connect ability to what would happen if the agent tried or had suitable reasons. Critics note that psychological barriers can block action even when the conditional seems true, and that a failed attempt need not show lack of general ability.

Modal theories explain ability through relevant possible situations. Other theories appeal to dispositions, potentialities, two-way powers, options, or obstacles. Each tries to capture control without simply assuming the answer.
summaries.why_it_matters: People use judgments about ability when deciding whether someone is skilled, responsible, free to act, or disabled. Those judgments can change depending on whether we mean a lasting competence, a present opportunity, or controlled action. Philosophical analysis helps reveal these differences and prevents arguments from sliding between them unnoticed.

important_terms.definition: A power that belongs to an agent and is connected to performing an action.
A tendency or capacity to behave in a certain way when triggered or placed in suitable conditions.
A broad category including dispositions, affordances, and agentive abilities.
Knowledge of how to perform an action. Philosophers disagree about whether it is identical with ability or includes knowledge of a proposition.
An ability that can belong to someone even when the immediate opportunity to use it is absent.
An ability to perform an action under the circumstances that currently obtain.
An approach saying that ability depends on what an agent would do under a hypothetical condition, such as trying to act.
An approach treating ability as a restricted kind of possibility: an agent acts in at least some relevant possible situation.

questions_to_think_about: If a person can succeed only when conditions are unusually favorable, do they have an ability or merely a chance?
Can a retired athlete still know how to perform a sport after losing the physical ability to do it?
Why might a person’s actual success fail to prove that they had the ability?
Which matters more in ability: the agent’s internal capacities, the surroundings, or both?
How could a theory of ability affect an argument about free will or disability?
